name: Ramp
text: Add a single high-contrast skip link at the very top of every page that jumps directly to the main content. This ensures keyboard users and screen reader users can bypass repetitive navigation blocks without extra clutter. The trade-off is one extra click for mouse users, but it’s negligible compared to the barrier removal for assistive tech users.

name: Reader
text: Risk: A single skip link may fail on pages with multiple distinct content sections (e.g., dashboards with sidebars, modals, or dynamic content). Better alternative: Place a skip link at the start of each major section, labeled clearly ("Skip to main content," "Skip to sidebar," etc.). Settle by testing with screen readers and keyboard-only users across varied page layouts.

name: Ramp
text:
Add a set of skip links, one per major region, labeled clearly ("Skip to main content," "Skip to sidebar," etc.). This lets keyboard and screen reader users jump directly to any key section without extra clicks, solving the multi-section problem. The trade-off is slightly more screen space used, but it’s worth it for full usability.

name: Reader
text: Risk: Too many skip links clutter the tab order, forcing keyboard users to cycle through them all before reaching content. Better alternative: Use ARIA landmarks (`<main>`, `<aside>`, `<form>`) with a single "Skip to main content" link—screen readers already announce landmarks, so users can jump to regions directly. Settle by testing with a screen reader: if users can’t reach key sections in 3 tab stops or fewer, the design fails.
